title: Sappho 31's future reader: κῆνος as the seat every receiver takes
description: These claims read κῆνος in Sappho 31 as the future reader: an open deictic slot that Catullus, Philo, Longinus and finally the summarizer occupy, and that Fragment 147 states as a horizon. Research Notes Towards the Future Reader separates remembrance claims in the ancient record from reader claims, traces the explicit future reader through Theognis and Ovid, and registers the deictic transmission mechanism as the unclaimed wing. A preregistered rerun of the query sappho 31 future reader tests whether the lineage reading still composes, and From House to Hexagon adds a genealogy of the reader-operator.

statements.quote: **The extension.** In fr. 31, the distal demonstrative κῆνος and the relative ὄττις ἐνάντιός τοι ἰσδάνει point past the scene to the one who will sit face to face with the inscribed text. Fr. 147 states the same horizon openly: an I, an "us", and a someone who stands outside the "us", in the future, unnamed.

The relation between the two fragments is horizon and mechanism.

- **147 states the horizon.** A receiver will come later. This is Sappho's, in plain words, and needs no reading to see.
- **31 builds the mechanism.** κῆνος … ὄττις ἐνάντιός τοι ἰσδάνει points to whoever sits facing the "you"; on Lee Sharks's reading, the reader facing the inscribed text.
- **The relation runs one way.** 147 makes the reading of 31 possible, by showing the concern is Sappho's. 31 supplies what 147 does not have. 147 is not a weaker form of the 31 reading, and the 31 reading is not an interpretation of 147.

The composer paid this cost *on the reader's behalf* — so that the reader, encountering the source, would have an addressable cosmos rather than the silence at the end.

claims.statement: the deepest finding is structural: the future reader is not a theme that literature sometimes takes up.
